title: Helm releases through Terraform

story: A bug in the broker made Nova's pushes fail now and then, and the fix is merged. The new image is built and waiting in the registry. It is late, so a teammate runs kubectl set image on inf to put the new image on the broker directly. It works, the errors stop, and everybody goes home.

Two weeks later, someone changes the broker's replica count the normal way, through the infrastructure repo, and a person applies it. The plan for that change said nothing about images. But after the apply the broker is running the old image again, the push errors are back, and nobody can see why, because the only record of the new image was a command typed in a terminal two weeks ago.
hook.question: How does a new version of a service reach inf so that the change is written down, reviewed, and cannot quietly disappear?

read.h: A chart is YAML with holes in it
p: In the last lesson you read a Deployment and a Service for the broker. The gateway, the orchestrator worker and the Slack app need almost the same two objects, with a different name, image and replica count. Copying the YAML four times would mean four places to fix every mistake, so instead we write it once as a Helm chart. A chart is a folder of Kubernetes YAML templates with holes in them, written as {{ .Values.something }}, plus a values.yaml file with a default for every hole. Helm is the tool that fills the holes and sends the result to the cluster.

If you know React, this will feel familiar: the templates are the component, the values are its props, and helm template is the render. The comparison stops at the output. A render goes to a screen and is gone, but Helm sends objects to a cluster and remembers each install as a release, with a numbered revision for every change, so it can show you the history and go back to an older revision.

code.file: a chart made with helm create, and one render of it
code.text:
# ai-agents-service/templates/deployment.yaml (two of its lines)
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"

# ai-agents-service/values.yaml (the defaults)
replicaCount: 1
image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: ""

# render it, with our values instead of the defaults
helm template broker ./ai-agents-service -n ai-agents \
  --set replicaCount=2 --set image.tag=1.27@sha256:6784fb08…

notes.text: A hole. Helm puts the value of replicaCount here.
Two holes in one line. The real file also falls back to the chart's version when tag is empty; that part is left out here.
The defaults. Our values replace only what we need, the way props replace default props.
helm template only prints the filled-in YAML. It never touches a cluster, so it is always safe to run.
The tag holds a readable version and the digest after the @. The digest decides which image runs; the 1.27 is for people.

read.h: On inf, Terraform installs the chart
p: You could install a chart yourself with helm install. On inf nobody does, for the reason in the story: a command typed in a terminal leaves no record that anyone reviews. Instead, every tool on inf, from Vault and n8n to our agent services, is a Terraform unit in the infrastructure repo. You met units in p4-2: one folder, one state, one plan. For a service on inf, the unit uses a resource called helm_release, which comes from Terraform's Helm provider and does what helm install and helm upgrade do, but from code. The product clusters use a different tool, Argo CD, and none of its apps point at inf.

All our agent services share one small local chart and one module around it, so the broker's unit only has to say its name, its replica count and its image. Below is the heart of that module. Notice that the chart sits inside the module folder: changing the chart is a pull request too.

notes.text: The release name. Helm keeps this release's revisions in the cluster under this name.
A chart stored next to the module, not downloaded from the internet, so it changes only through a reviewed PR.
yamlencode turns a Terraform map into YAML, so the values are written in HCL and arrive at Helm as YAML.
The broker's unit passes the image from our registry with its digest, for example …/ai-agents-broker@sha256:… .

deeper.h: Go deeper: a service with a database, the n8n way
p: A service that needs more than pods gets more units in its folder. n8n set the pattern on inf: a secrets unit that generates the database password straight into Vault, an sg unit with a security group that lets only inf reach Postgres, an rds unit that creates the database, and a repository unit with the helm_release. Units depend on each other with dependency blocks, so the repository unit reads the database address from the rds unit's outputs. Our own Temporal on inf is built exactly this way, with the upstream Temporal chart instead of our small one.

Some values can only be chosen once. Temporal's numHistoryShards, which splits its work into a fixed number of parts, is written into the database at the first install and can never change afterwards. A plan that changes it looks harmless, but the server would refuse to start. That is why such numbers are decided in the ticket and marked with a comment in the code, not tuned later.

read.h: The plan is the review, and the code is the only owner
p: Now a new broker image is a one-line change: the digest in the broker's unit. The author runs a plan, pastes it into the pull request, and the reviewer sees exactly what will happen before anything does. Here is the plan for such a change, from the lab you are about to do. One line goes, one line comes, and nothing else moves. After approval a person applies it, never an agent, and Helm records a new revision while the Deployment replaces the pods one by one.

The story at the top is the other half of this rule. A change made with kubectl does not appear in any plan, because Terraform compares the code with what it applied last time, not with the live pods. In the lab you will see a plan answer "No changes" while the cluster runs a different image. This difference between the code and what really runs is called drift. Then, at the next apply for any reason, Helm writes the whole recipe from the code again, and the hand-made change is gone without a word. So on inf the code is the only owner of a service, and the way to change a service is to change its code.
read.see:
~ resource "helm_release" "broker" {
      ~ values = [
          ~ <<-EOT
                "image":
              -   "tag": "1.27@sha256:6784fb08…"
              +   "tag": "1.28@sha256:146adea4…"
                "replicaCount": 2
Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.

lab.title: Ship a new image with a plan
needs: The laptop cluster from p5-1 (or its first two steps again)
lab.goal: Install a chart into your laptop cluster with a Terraform helm_release, ship a new image by changing one digest, and see why a change made by hand gets lost.

guess.q: The broker is running image A, installed by Terraform. Someone changes it to image B with kubectl set image. You run tofu plan without changing any code. What does the plan say?

options.text: 1 to change: it wants to put image A back.
options.why: That would be nice, but Terraform compares your code with what it applied last time, and neither of those changed. It never looked at the live pods.

options.text: No changes, while the cluster runs image B.
options.why: The plan cannot see the hand-made change. That is what makes such changes dangerous: they are invisible until the next apply quietly removes them.

options.text: An error, because the cluster no longer matches the state file.
options.why: Nothing fails. The difference stays hidden, which is worse than an error.

follow.say: Start from a clean laptop cluster. If you stopped it, docker start academy brings it back; then remove the hand-made objects from p5-1, because from now on only code owns what runs.
follow.do: docker start academy && export KUBECONFIG=~/academy-k3s.yaml && kubectl get nodes && kubectl delete namespace ai-agents --ignore-not-found
follow.see:
academy
NAME      STATUS   ROLES                  AGE   VERSION
academy   Ready    control-plane,master   12m   v1.33.5+k3s1
namespace "ai-agents" deleted

follow.say: Make a chart. helm create writes a complete small chart for a web server, which is close to what our shared service chart looks like.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p5-2 && cd ~/academy-labs/p5-2 && helm create ai-agents-service && grep -n -E 'replicas:|image:' ai-agents-service/templates/deployment.yaml

follow.say: Render it with our values before anything touches a cluster, so you see exactly what would be created.
follow.do: helm template broker ./ai-agents-service -n ai-agents --set fullnameOverride=broker --set replicaCount=2 --set image.tag=1.27@sha256:6784fb0834aa7dbbe12e3d7471e69c290df3e6ba810dc38b34ae33d3c1c05f7d | grep -E '^kind:|replicas:|image:'

follow.say: Write the Terraform for the release. The provider points at your laptop cluster's key file, and the image is one local value, so a new image will be a one-line change.

lab.build: Give the gateway and the Slack app their own releases from the same chart, the way the shared module gives every agent service its own unit. Add a local gateway_image (use the 1.28 image), then two helm_release resources: gateway with 2 replicas and slack-app with 1, each with its own fullnameOverride. Run tofu plan and check that it says 2 to add, 0 to change, then apply and list the releases with helm -n ai-agents list.
checks: helm template prints an image line that ends with the sha256 digest you passed
The first tofu plan says Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
After you change broker_image, the plan shows one line with - and one with +, and says 1 to change
helm -n ai-agents history broker shows revision 2 with Upgrade complete
After the hand-made kubectl change, tofu plan says No changes, and the next apply puts the 1.28 digest back
helm -n ai-agents list shows broker, gateway and slack-app as deployed
lab.fix: A teammate wanted to test the gateway before its unit existed, so they made its Service by hand with kubectl -n ai-agents create service clusterip gateway --tcp=80:80 and forgot it. Run that command before your build step's apply, and the apply fails with Service "gateway" in namespace "ai-agents" exists and cannot be imported into the current release. Read the message: who owns that Service today, and who should? Repair it so that Terraform is the only owner, and apply again until helm list shows the gateway.
explain: Why does a chart have both templates and a values.yaml, and what did --set change in your render?
Why did tofu plan say No changes while the cluster ran a different image, and what removed that image later?
Why does the broker's image line carry a digest, and what does a reviewer see in the plan when the broker gets a new image?
lab.done: A one-line digest change produced a one-line plan and a new Helm revision, the hand-made change was invisible to the plan and lost at the next apply, and three releases from one chart run in ai-agents.

check.q: The broker needs a new image on inf today. What is the right way?

options.text: kubectl set image on inf, then open a PR with the same change so the code matches later
options.why: For a while the cluster and the code disagree, and the plan cannot see it. If anyone applies another change from older code in between, the new image is silently replaced.

options.text: Change the digest in the broker's unit, paste the plan into the PR, and a person applies after approval
options.why: The change is written down, reviewed as a one-line plan, and becomes a Helm revision. The code stays the only owner of the service.

options.text: Ask Nova to apply the change, since it has the plan already
options.why: Agents never apply. An agent may write the change and show a plan that a person produced; the apply is always a person's action.

options.text: It installs the chart into whichever cluster kubectl points at
options.why: That is helm install, and mixing the two up is a classic way to install something into the wrong cluster.

options.text: It downloads the images the chart needs
options.why: Helm never touches images. The nodes download them when pods start.

options.text: It fills the chart's templates with values and prints the YAML, without touching any cluster
options.why: That is why it is safe to run anywhere, and why it is the first thing to run when you want to know what a chart will create.

check.q: Someone fixed the broker by hand with kubectl last week. Today an unrelated replica change is applied from the infrastructure repo. What happens to last week's fix?

options.text: It stays, because the plan only mentioned replicas
options.why: The plan only showed what changed in the code. The apply still sends the whole recipe from the code, including the old image.

options.text: It disappears, because Helm writes the whole recipe from the code again
options.why: The code never knew about the fix, so the upgrade puts the code's version back. That is the story at the top of this lesson.

options.text: The apply fails with a conflict, so someone notices
options.why: No conflict is raised. The fix is replaced without a word, which is why hand changes are so dangerous.

p: On inf, every tool is a Terraform helm_release unit in the infrastructure repo, and no Argo CD app points at inf; Argo CD and the gitops repo serve the product clusters only. The agent services follow the n8n pattern under multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/: one folder per service (llm-gateway, broker, orchestrator-worker, slack-app), each a unit on the shared module modules/ai-agents-service, which wraps a small local chart with the Deployment, the Service, the ExternalSecret and a VMServiceScrape for metrics. Images come from our ECR repositories, which refuse to move a tag, and the units pin them by digest. The Helm and Kubernetes providers are pinned in the root config (helm 3.1.1, kubernetes 3.0.1).

Our Temporal is the same pattern with more units: secrets, sg, rds and repository, with the upstream Temporal chart 1.5.0, a db.t4g.small Postgres with deletion protection and 14-day backups, and numHistoryShards 128, chosen once for good. Today the author plans over VPN and pastes the plan into the PR; a later ticket posts read-only plans on infrastructure PRs automatically. Either way a person applies.

tickets.why: Creates modules/ai-agents-service and the first unit on it, the LLM gateway.
The broker, orchestrator worker and Slack app as units on the same module, images pinned by digest.
Our Temporal on inf: secrets, sg, rds and repository units, and the upstream chart as a helm_release.
The brain bot's unit: the smallest example, with the digest kept in one .hcl file.
Read-only Terragrunt plans posted on infrastructure PRs, so reviewers no longer depend on a pasted plan.

words.plain: A folder of Kubernetes YAML templates with holes, plus a values.yaml with a default for every hole.
The inputs that fill a chart's holes, like props for a component.
One install of a chart in a cluster, with a numbered revision for every change.
The Terraform resource that installs or upgrades a chart from code, so the change shows in a plan.
A difference between what runs and what the code says, usually from a change made by hand.

review.q: Write the three things the broker's unit tells the shared module, and say which one changes when the broker gets a new image.
review.a: Its name, its replica count and its image with a digest. A new image changes only the digest, which is a one-line plan.

review.q: A teammate says: "I used kubectl set image on inf, but I also opened the PR, so it is fine." What can still go wrong before the PR is applied?
review.a: Any apply from code that does not have the change yet puts the old image back without a word, and the plan in between shows No changes, so nobody notices.

review.q: Why do some values, like Temporal's shard count, get a comment in the code saying they cannot change?
review.a: They are fixed at the first install. A later plan would look harmless but break the service, so the decision is made once, in the ticket, and marked.

remember: On inf a service changes only through its code: a chart filled with values, installed by a helm_release, shown as a plan and applied by a person.
